strengths: Clear problem formulation: the paper defines skill-based continual learning via three properties (P1 no weight updates, P2 compositional transfer with OOD skills, P3 zero-shot multi-skill composition), giving a crisp framework the experiments are organized around.

The central idea—learning vocabulary-level soft tokens on skill-centered datasets to encode procedural knowledge—is a novel and promising angle, building naturally on the Arora & Goyal skill formalism and Hewitt et al.'s neologisms, and is well differentiated from prompt tuning, LoRA, and meaningful-soft-token prior work.
Section 4 (XOR/XNOR keyword study) is a clever and intuitive motivation showing that some pretrained tokens already act as skill tokens, providing empirical grounding for the approach.

The controlled synthetic setting allows exact ID/OOD splits over skills, and the main comparison is reasonably fair: Prompt Tuning is matched to Skill Neologisms in soft token count (17,920 params), and in-context learning is included as a natural zero-shot composition baseline.
Useful ablations on token length (capacity as inductive bias), training composition complexity, and initialization, with detailed breakdowns in the appendix.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: hyperparameters, dataset construction, test-set generation, hardware, and frameworks are documented across appendices D–E, and limitations (dataset construction cost, soft-token optimization instability, computational cost of backprop through the full model, proof-of-concept scope) are honestly discussed in Appendix C.
weaknesses: The continual learning claim in the title and abstract is never directly evaluated: only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) are learned, with no sequential acquisition of multiple skills over time and no measurement of interference or forgetting across successive skill additions. The evidence supports a compositional-transfer result, not continual learning.

The experimental scope is very narrow for an ICML main-track contribution: a single small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B), synthetic digit-sequence operations, and skills that are literally explicit operation markers ([SHIFT], [INV-POL]). The insertion function simply swaps the operation token, so the task reduces to learning an embedding for an already-explicit skill symbol—far from the natural-language skill scenario the framing motivates. Moreover, the 'pretrained' base model is itself LoRA-fine-tuned by the authors, weakening the analogy to real pretrained LLMs.

Section 4 has an unaddressed confound: the failure of the 'XNOR' keyword may be explained by tokenization (XNOR likely tokenizes differently than the single familiar 'XOR' token) rather than absence of procedural knowledge, and the Google NGram frequency argument is anecdotal. The experiment uses only one task pair and N=100 samples per condition.

Evaluation fairness concerns: Table E3 shows the ICL baseline in Figure 5 is evaluated at temperature 1 while the main experiments use greedy decoding—an inconsistent protocol in the head-to-head comparison. Additionally, P3 is tested only for Skill Neologisms vs. ICL; composing two independently trained Prompt Tuning prefixes zero-shot is never tested, so the claim that prefix methods are 'structurally unable to achieve P3' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Figure 4 and Figure 6 report single-run results without error bars or multiple seeds, despite the acknowledged instability of soft-token optimization (Appendix C); Table 5's high variances (e.g., .36 ± .44) suggest substantial run-to-run variability that the single-seed figures may not represent.

Some sloppiness undermines confidence: incomplete sentences ('In this work, investigate whether...'), typos ('as well as a other skills', 'different a given Sheld-out'), a duplicated/incorrect appendix heading (A.5 labeled as composition-complexity but containing initialization results), and inconsistent description of the Prompt Tuning implementation ('simply inserting soft tokens before every prompt').

strengths: The problem formulation is crisp and well-motivated: the paper clearly defines 'skill-based continual learning' via three testable properties (P1: no weight updates, P2: compositional transfer with OOD skills, P3: zero-shot composition of independently learned skills), building on the formalism of Arora & Goyal (2023).

The core idea—training vocabulary-integrated soft tokens on skill-centered datasets while keeping the model frozen—is simple, sensible, and clearly distinguished from prompt tuning and prefix methods (Table 1, Section 3.5).

The experimental design in Section 5 is carefully controlled: explicit ID/OOD skill splits, permutation-based test generation, multiple baselines (LoRA, Prompt Tuning, ICL), and detailed ablations over token length, training composition complexity, and initialization.
Reproducibility is strong: appendices provide full hyperparameter tables (E1–E7), dataset construction details, prompt templates, and hardware specifications.

The limitations discussion (Appendix C) is honest and substantive, acknowledging the proof-of-concept scope, soft-token optimization instability, dataset construction challenges, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is very narrow relative to the central claims. All main results use a single 0.5B model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on a synthetic digit-operation task, with only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL). The abstract and conclusion claims about 'a scalable path towards skill-based continual learning' rest on this toy setting; no natural-language, real-world, or larger-model experiments are provided.

The motivating experiment in Section 4 is weak. It evaluates only XOR vs. XNOR with N=100 samples, and the conclusion (that 'XOR' tokens encode procedural knowledge) has plausible alternative explanations (tokenization, output-format priors, frequency effects) that are not controlled for. The negative XNOR result is also left largely unexplained.

Absolute zero-shot composition performance is modest and overstated in the takeaways. Figure 5 shows skill neologism accuracy degrading from ~0.6 to ~0.2 as sequence length grows, with large variance and near-zero results for some held-out skills (e.g., ID in Figure A3); 'successfully composed zero-shot' is a generous characterization.

Missing comparisons with the closest related methods. ToolkenGPT (Hao et al., 2023) and steering tokens (Radevski et al., 2026) learn vocabulary-level tokens for frozen LLMs, yet neither is empirically compared despite being acknowledged; the originality claim ('first to learn composable soft tokens for procedural knowledge') is asserted rather than demonstrated against these baselines.

The claimed advantage of Skill Neologisms over Prompt Tuning (same trainable parameter count) is empirically observed but mechanistically unexplained; the paper offers only speculation about 'additional flexibility', and there is no analysis of what the learned tokens actually represent.

Several presentation defects reduce polish: the A.5 appendix heading mislabels the initialization ablation as 'Effect of compositions'; E.5.1/E.5.2 refer to an incomplete 'Section under the Skill Neologisms column'; the introduction is missing a subject ('In this work, investigate whether...'); and Table 3's SHIFT example ([SHIFT]472=247) is confusingly identical to the ASC example.

Key results show notable variance across configurations (e.g., INV-POL C2 accuracy jumps from .36 to .85 depending on training complexity, with std up to .44), and the robustness of the approach in realistic settings where skills are implicit and data noisy remains entirely open.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper defines skill-based continual learning via three concrete properties (P1 no weight updates, P2 compositional transfer with OOD skills, P3 zero-shot composition of independently learned skills), which makes the claims testable.

The synthetic experimental design is carefully controlled: explicit sample-skill mappings, clean ID/OOD splits over both held-out skills and held-out sequence lengths, and test sets that enumerate all operation orderings, which guards against memorization of specific compositions.

Fair baseline comparisons with matched parameter budgets: Skill Neologisms and Prompt Tuning both use 20 soft tokens (17,920 trainable parameters), making the OOD generalization gap (e.g., 0.75 vs 0.28 OOD accuracy for SHIFT) a meaningful apples-to-apples result.

Useful ablations on token length (showing an inverted-U capacity effect on OOD accuracy), training composition complexity (k_max), and initialization, which provide genuine insight into the mechanism rather than only headline numbers.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Appendix C covers dataset construction, scope, soft-token instabilities, and computational cost), plus extensive hyperparameter documentation (Tables E1–E7) that supports reproducibility.
The Section 4 observation that common tokens like 'XOR' function as de facto skill tokens while rare tokens like 'XNOR' do not is a nice, simple motivating experiment across four open-source models.
weaknesses: Scope of evidence is narrow: all main claims rest on a single small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) and only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) on a synthetic digit-operation task. There is no evidence that the approach works on natural language skills or larger models, so the 'towards skill-based continual learning' framing rests heavily on extrapolation.

The Section 4 motivating experiment is weak evidence for its conclusion: N=100 samples, and the XOR-vs-XNOR keyword advantage could be confounded (e.g., 'XOR' co-occurs with explicit descriptions in pretraining text, so the keyword may act as a retrieval cue rather than evidence of a standalone procedural 'skill token'). The causal interpretation is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Zero-shot multi-skill composition (P3) is demonstrated for only a single pair of skills, and absolute performance is modest and high-variance (Figure 5 accuracies of ~0.2–0.6, declining with sequence length; individual held-out runs range widely). This is far from compelling evidence for scalable continual learning.

The mechanistic explanation for why Skill Neologisms beat Prompt Tuning with identical token counts ('semantically embedding the soft tokens inside the prompts may provide additional flexibility') is speculative; no probing or analysis is offered to explain the difference, and the claimed inductive bias from 'limited parameter capacity' is not directly tested against the LoRA result.

Some results have large variance that weakens conclusions (e.g., INV-POL C2 OOD of .36 ± .44 at k_max=1 in Table 5; Table A1 shows several near-zero entries), and the paper averages across settings where individual runs differ dramatically.

Practical relevance of the insertion function is unexamined: in the experiments the soft tokens simply replace an existing '[SHIFT]' label token, which presumes the skill is already explicitly marked in the input—this does not obviously transfer to real tasks where the required skill is implicit, and the paper does not test the more realistic insertion modes it describes in Table 2.

Presentation issues: minor grammatical errors ('In this work, investigate whether...'), a reference to a '(D)' panel in Figure 2 that does not exist, and duplicated section titles in the appendix (A.4/A.5 both 'Effect of compositions in training set'). No explicit code-release statement, which limits reproducibility despite good hyperparameter documentation.

strengths: The problem is clearly formulated: the paper defines skill-based continual learning via three properties (P1: no weight updates, P2: compositional transfer to OOD skills, P3: zero-shot multi-skill composition), making the claims falsifiable and the comparison to fine-tuning and prefix-based methods (Table 1) transparent.

The controlled algorithmic setup (Section 5) is well designed: exact ID/OOD splits over skills, leave-one-out held-out skills, permutation-controlled test generation, and multiple runs (12 per method) allow a clean measurement of compositional transfer rather than task memorization.

The ablations are informative and well-motivated: skill-token length reveals a capacity/generalization trade-off (Figure 6), training composition complexity (Table 5) and label noise (Figure A4) probe the inductive-bias hypothesis, and initialization ablations (Table 6) show the method is not overly initialization-sensitive.

Skill neologisms beat prompt tuning with the same number of soft tokens (17,920 parameters) on OOD compositions (Figure 4), which is a meaningful controlled comparison isolating the effect of vocabulary-level integration vs. prefixing.

The experimental appendices are unusually thorough (models, hyperparameters, dataset generation, hardware), and the limitations discussion (Appendix C) is honest about dataset construction, soft-token instability, and computational cost.
The observation that pretrained models already exhibit skill-associated tokens (Section 4) is a nice motivating experiment connecting the method to naturally occurring behavior.
weaknesses: Scale and generality are limited. The main experiments use only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) on a 0.5B model, and the natural-language validation uses only two skills from Skill-Mix with a 3B model and 50 test queries, single-run with no variance reported. The central claims rest on a very small number of skill instances.

The central 'continual learning' claim (P1 preventing catastrophic forgetting) is asserted but never measured: the paper never evaluates whether the base model retains its other skills or general capabilities when a neologism is present in context. For a paper titled 'towards skill-based continual learning', the absence of any forgetting/interference evaluation is a notable evidential gap.

There is a mismatch between the motivating claim and the main experiments. Section 4 argues pretrained LLMs naturally have skill tokens, but the main experiments (Section 5) use a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B on synthetic digit operations as the 'pretrained' model; the behavior of neologisms on genuinely pretrained skills is only touched via the small Skill-Mix experiment.

The Skill-Mix experiment (Section 6) is confounded: the prompt template (Listing 1/Appendix D.3.2) still includes the full textual definitions and one example for each queried skill alongside the soft tokens, so the marginal contribution of the neologisms over the rich in-context description is unclear; accuracy differences between methods in Figure 7 are modest and reported without confidence intervals, and grading by GPT-5 introduces additional noise.

The motivating Section 4 result is thin: two operations (XOR/XNOR), N=100 samples, and the interpretation is confounded—e.g., the text description hurting XOR accuracy is surprising and unexplained, and frequency on Google NGram is only anecdotal support for the mechanism.

Reproducibility is weakened by placeholder code links: the paper states 'Code to reproduce our experiments can be found at' followed by empty URLs on both page 2 and page 16 (appendix D). Without the code, exact replication of the custom soft-token training would be difficult.

Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially Hewitt et al.'s neologism embedding learning applied with skill-centered training data; the closest concurrent work (Radevski et al., 2026, composable steering tokens) is acknowledged, and the positioning as 'the first' for procedural knowledge is defensible but narrow.

Presentation issues: several figures (Figure 6's value labels, Figure A3) are hard to read, and the capability gaps across methods sometimes fluctuate substantially across held-out skills (e.g., Table A1 shows INV-POL with kmax=1 near 0.00 accuracy on several held-out skills), suggesting high variance that the averaged tables partially obscure.

strengths: The problem formulation is clear and well-motivated: the three properties (P1 no weight updates, P2 compositional transfer to OOD skills, P3 zero-shot multi-skill composition) crisply define what skill-based continual learning would require, and the paper is explicit about which property each experiment tests.

The controlled synthetic setting (digit-sequence transformations with explicit skill labels) is well designed for cleanly measuring OOD skill composition, with leave-one-out skill splits, permutation-based test generation, and held-out sequence lengths, and the appendix provides unusually detailed experimental configurations.

The paper includes useful ablations (skill token length, composition complexity in training data, initialization, label noise) that go beyond a simple proof-of-concept, and the finding that limited token capacity acts as an inductive bias for composability is interesting.

The limitations discussion (Appendix C) is honest and substantive, covering dataset construction difficulty, soft-token optimization instability, and computational cost, and the work is explicitly framed as a proof-of-concept rather than a finished solution.
Validating zero-shot composition of independently learned skill tokens on Skill-Mix connects the controlled findings to a more realistic natural language setting.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited. Skill neologisms are essentially prompt tuning soft tokens with (a) skill-centered training data and (b) insertion mid-prompt rather than as a prefix. Since the prompt tuning baseline in Table D2 is trained on the same skill-centered data with the same token budget, the reported gap appears attributable to insertion position alone; there is no ablation isolating this (e.g., prompt tuning with the same insertion function, or a discrete [SKILL] token replaced by a learned embedding), which makes the contribution's mechanism hard to attribute.

The 'first to propose learning composable soft tokens that encapsulate procedural knowledge' claim is overstated given closely related prior work the paper itself cites (ToolkenGPT for tool tokens in vocabulary, Radevski et al. for composable steering tokens, Textual Inversion for grounded pseudo-words).

Section 4 (existence of natural skill tokens) is weak evidence: only one operation pair (XOR/XNOR), four models, an anecdotal NGram frequency argument, and no control for the keyword acting as a generic task cue rather than encoding procedural knowledge. This motivational experiment does not reliably support the takeaway.

The baseline comparison is potentially unfair in capacity: LoRA has ~2.9M trainable parameters versus ~18k for the soft-token methods. The dramatic LoRA failure on OOD composition could be a capacity/overfitting artifact rather than evidence for the proposed mechanism; a capacity-matched LoRA is missing.

Scale and generality are limited: the synthetic experiments use a 0.5B model, and the natural language validation covers only one 3B model, two target skills, and 50 test queries graded by a single GPT-5 judge with no statistical significance testing or agreement analysis. Claims of a 'scalable path' toward continual learning are not supported at scale.

In the Skill-Mix setup, the full skill definitions and examples remain in the prompt alongside the inserted neologisms, so the marginal contribution of the learned soft tokens over the definitions themselves is unclear; a definitions-only or neologism-only ablation is absent.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code availability statements on pages 2 and 16 are incomplete, with empty URL placeholders ('Code to reproduce our experiments can be found at' followed by nothing).

Some reported results have internal inconsistencies or are under-analyzed, e.g., large variance in Table 5 (±.44, ±.34 for k_max=1,2) and zero/very low OOD accuracies for several held-out skills in Table A1 (SUB, ID) that are glossed over in the takeaway narrative, suggesting the method fails for some skill combinations in ways the main text does not confront.

strengths: The paper articulates a clear, well-motivated problem formulation (skill-based continual learning with properties P1–P3) and positions it cleanly against fine-tuning, prompt tuning, and in-context approaches (Table 1).

The controlled synthetic setting (digit-sequence transformations) is well designed: explicit sample-skill mappings, leave-one-out skill splits, permutation-inclusive test sets, and held-out sequence lengths allow a clean measurement of compositional transfer (P2) that most PEFT comparisons lack.
The motivating experiment in Section 4 (XOR vs. XNOR keyword probing across four open-source models) is a clever and novel observation that naturally motivates vocabulary-level skill parameters.

The comparison to prompt tuning is fair and informative: both methods optimize the same number of soft tokens on the same skill-centered data, isolating the effect of vocabulary-level insertion vs. prefix insertion, which is a genuinely useful ablation for the field.

Ablations are thorough and insightful: token-length capacity trade-off (Figure 6), composition complexity in training data (Table 5), initialization sensitivity (Table 6), and label-noise robustness (Figure A4) collectively advance understanding of when and why the method works.

The paper is honest about its limitations (Appendix C: dataset construction burden, soft-token optimization instability, computational cost of backpropagating through the full model), which is appreciated and does not overclaim.
Experimental details are extensive (Appendix D), covering configurations, test-set generation procedures, and hardware, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scale of evidence is limited: the core algorithmic experiments use Qwen2.5-0.5B, and the only natural-language validation uses Llama-3.2-3B with just two target skills and 50 test queries on Skill-Mix, graded by GPT-5 at temperature 1.0 with minimal reasoning effort. At this sample size, differences in Figure 7 have wide confidence intervals and the generality of P3 in natural language remains weakly supported.

Property 3 is only demonstrated for composing two independently learned neologisms (synthetic and Skill-Mix). True continual learning would require composing many neologisms simultaneously; interference or degradation with larger token collections is untested, so the 'scalable path' framing is not yet substantiated.

Section 4's evidence that pretrained tokens encapsulate procedural knowledge rests on a single operation pair (XOR/XNOR) with N=100 samples per condition. The frequency confound is acknowledged via an NGram count but not experimentally controlled (e.g., additional rare/common operation pairs), so the claim that keyword exposure drives skill-token emergence is suggestive rather than established.

P2 (compositional transfer) is not validated on natural language; the Skill-Mix experiment only covers zero-shot combination of two neologisms, so the paper's central continual-learning claim rests almost entirely on the synthetic digit task.

Training data for Skill-Mix is generated by GPT-5, meaning the 'new skill' acquisition is largely distillation of a stronger model's existing capability; a baseline comparing against GPT-5-generated few-shot examples or skill descriptions alone would clarify how much the neologism mechanism itself contributes.

Novelty is moderate: the method combines prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021) with vocabulary-level neologisms (Hewitt et al., 2025) plus a data-curation perspective (skill-centered datasets), and the closest work on composable steering tokens (Radevski et al., 2026) is cited only briefly; a deeper empirical or conceptual differentiation would strengthen the contribution.

Presentation flaws: the code availability statement appears twice with an incomplete URL ('can be found at' with nothing following), and Figure 4's rendering makes some bars difficult to interpret; Table 1's claim that prefix-based methods cannot achieve P3 is asserted structurally but never empirically tested for prefix-based methods under their skill-centered training recipe.

The paper frames itself as continual learning, but never measures performance of the base model's existing skills after neologisms are added in combination (e.g., whether inserting two neologisms degrades unrelated skill performance), which is the core metric of the field it targets.
